analysis.one_liner: Requires the Supreme Court to write and publish a code of conduct and handle ethics complaints about its justices.
analysis.headline: The Supreme Court Code of Conduct Act, backed by two senators, died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Supreme Court to write its own code of conduct for the nine justices, publish it publicly, and designate someone to receive complaints about justices' conduct. Complaints would be summarized publicly each year, and investigators could be brought in to look into alleged misconduct. Lower federal judges already live under a code of conduct; the bill would have extended the same basic idea to the Supreme Court.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who appear before, or are affected by, Supreme Court rulings: the bill would have given the public a written standard for justices' behavior, a place to file complaints, and an annual public accounting of complaints and any remedial steps taken.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Any citizen affected by Court rulings

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required the Supreme Court to issue a code of conduct for the Chief Justice and the associate justices within one year, with public notice and comment.
The code would have had to be published on the Court's website so the public could read the rules justices are held to.

The Court would have had to designate an individual to process misconduct complaints about justices, and publish an annual public report of those complaints (with complainants' names removed) and any steps taken in response.
The Marshal of the Supreme Court could have commissioned federal investigators or outside contractors to investigate alleged misconduct by a justice or a justice's employee.

analysis.who_pays: The nine Supreme Court justices, who would have become subject to a published code of conduct and a formal complaint process instead of relying on self-policing; the administrative cost would fall on the Court's own staff and budget.

drawbacks.text: The bill let the justices write their own code of conduct, so the rules would have been whatever a majority of the Court chose to adopt, with no outside body setting the standard.

The complaint process would have been run by an individual the Court itself designated, and any investigation could proceed only after consultation with the Chief Justice, so the Court would have policed itself rather than facing an independent investigator or any sanction mechanism.

The bill required the Court to designate a complaint processor but imposed no penalty for a justice found to have violated the code, so a skeptic could call it a transparency exercise rather than real accountability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a modest, low-cost step: it would not have taken power away from the Court or imposed penalties, but it would have replaced the justices' total silence on ethics rules with a public code, a complaint channel, and an annual public report. Its main weakness was that the Court would have written and administered the rules itself. As a first check on the only major court with no binding code of conduct, the benefit outweighed the cost, but it was a floor, not a full accountability regime.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the congressional term ended.

narrative.text: Senator Angus King introduced the bill on April 26, 2023, joined by Senator Lisa Murkowski.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.
No further action is listed: the committee never held a markup or vote, and the full Senate never considered the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nine Supreme Court justices came out ahead: they remain the only federal judges not subject to a binding code of conduct or a formal complaint process, because Congress never acted.

for.name: Angus King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Supreme Court Code of Conduct Act and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it; the action history shows no activity after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators backed the bill, an independent and a Republican; there is no recorded vote, so the partisan shape of any opposition never showed up on the record, though the Democratically led Judiciary Committee declined to move it.

industries.note: By dying without a vote, the bill left the nine justices as the only federal judges with no binding code of conduct or complaint process. The bill itself would have kept the Court in charge of writing and policing its own rules, so even its design favored institutional self-management.
